name: Senso-ji Temple
about: Senso-ji is Tokyo's oldest temple. According to tradition, two fishermen pulled a statue of Kannon from the Sumida River in 628, and the temple was completed in 645. The main hall and five-storied pagoda were destroyed in an air raid in 1945 and rebuilt in 1958 and 1973. Visitors enter through the Kaminarimon gate and walk along Nakamise-dori, a shopping street selling snacks and souvenirs, to reach the main hall.
hours: Main Hall 6:00-17:00 (Oct-Mar 6:30-17:00); grounds always open
price: Free
station: Asakusa Station (Ginza Line, Asakusa Line, Tobu Skytree Line)
car: Possible, but central Asakusa is crowded and public transport is easier

name: teamLab Planets TOKYO
name_ja: チームラボプラネッツ TOKYO
about: teamLab Planets is a digital art museum in Toyosu where visitors walk through water and rooms of light, mirrors and projections. Most of the artworks are meant to be experienced barefoot, so visitors take off shoes and socks, and trousers are rolled up for the water areas. Entry is by time-slot ticket bought in advance, and last entry is 60 minutes before closing.
hours: Varies by season and date, roughly 9:00-22:00 (last entry 60 minutes before closing); check the official calendar
closed: Irregular closures; check the official calendar
price: Adults about 3,800 yen (varies by date and time; child and youth prices are lower)
station: Shin-Toyosu Station (Yurikamome Line)
car: Not recommended; public transport is easier

name: Shibuya Scramble Crossing
name_ja: 渋谷スクランブル交差点
about: Shibuya Crossing is a pedestrian scramble in front of Shibuya Station, where traffic lights in all directions turn red at once and people cross from every side. It opened in 1973, and a 2016 report cited up to 3,000 pedestrians per green light. It is a common symbol of Tokyo in film and television. The Hachiko statue is nearby. Public drinking on the street is banned year-round from 6 p.m. to 5 a.m.
address: Near Shibuya Station Hachiko Exit, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo 150-0043
hours: Open 24 hours (public street)
price: Free
station: Shibuya Station (JR lines, Ginza Line, Hanzomon Line, Fukutoshin Line, Tokyu and Keio lines)
car: Not recommended; heavy traffic and no parking

name: Tokyo Skytree
about: Tokyo Skytree is a 634-meter broadcasting tower and the tallest structure in Japan. It has two observation decks, the Tembo Deck and the higher Tembo Galleria. The tower stands in Tokyo Skytree Town, which has shops, restaurants and an aquarium. Tickets can be bought in advance online or on the day at the ticket counter.
hours: 10:00-22:00 (last entry 21:00); varies by day
price: Price depends on the date. Tembo Deck adults from 1,800 yen online; combo ticket with Tembo Galleria from 3,000 yen; 500 yen more at the counter
station: Tokyo Skytree Station (Tobu Skytree Line); Oshiage Station (Hanzomon Line, Asakusa Line, Keisei Line)
car: Possible, but public transport is easier

name: Shinjuku Golden Gai
about: Golden Gai is a network of six narrow alleys with more than 200 tiny bars, clubs and eateries, many seating only a handful of people. The area developed into a drinking district after prostitution was outlawed in 1958, and some bars date to the 1960s. Most bars open from around 9 or 10 p.m. and many charge a cover. Many bars do not allow photos inside, so ask first.
hours: Mostly evening to late night; most bars open around 20:00-22:00 (each bar sets its own hours)
price: Drinks from about 800 yen; many bars charge a cover of about 500-1,500 yen (varies)
station: Shinjuku-sanchome Station (Marunouchi Line, Fukutoshin Line, Toei Shinjuku Line)
car: Not recommended; use public transport

name: Omoide Yokocho
about: Omoide Yokocho, also called Memory Lane, is a narrow alley of small yakitori, ramen and izakaya stalls beside the tracks near Shinjuku Station's west side. It grew out of the Shinjuku black market in the years just after World War II. Stalls are tiny and tightly packed, with counter seating. Most stalls open from about 5 p.m. to 11 p.m., and a few serve lunch.
hours: Mostly about 17:00-23:00; some stalls open from 11:00 (each stall sets its own hours)
price: Skewers from about 150-300 yen each; a meal about 2,000-4,000 yen (varies)
station: Shinjuku Station (JR lines, Marunouchi Line, Toei Oedo Line, Keio and Odakyu lines), West Exit
car: Not recommended; use public transport

name: Meiji Jingu
about: Meiji Jingu is a Shinto shrine dedicated to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken. It was established in 1920 and sits inside a forest of about 100,000 trees donated from across Japan. The shrine grounds are free to enter and open from sunrise to sunset, with the time changing by month. Visitors walk a long gravel path under large torii gates to the main shrine. The Inner Garden is a separate area with an entrance fee.
hours: Sunrise to sunset (e.g. January 6:40-16:20); changes by month
price: Free (Inner Garden 500 yen; museum 1,000 yen)
station: Harajuku Station (JR Yamanote Line); Meiji-jingumae Station (Chiyoda Line, Fukutoshin Line)
car: Not recommended; public transport is easier

name: Tsukiji Outer Market
about: The Tsukiji Outer Market is a group of retail shops and restaurants that remained in Tsukiji after the wholesale fish market moved to Toyosu. Its stalls sell fresh seafood, eggs, vegetables, dried foods and kitchenware, and many restaurants serve sushi and seafood rice bowls. Visitors often eat as they walk, with street snacks such as tamagoyaki and grilled seafood. Each shop sets its own hours.
hours: Varies by shop; many open about 5:00-14:00, with some open to 15:00
closed: Sundays and national holidays, plus some Wednesdays (varies by shop)
price: Free to walk; meals about 1,500-3,500 yen
station: Tsukiji Station (Hibiya Line); Tsukijishijo Station (Oedo Line)
car: Possible, but streets are busy and parking is limited

name: SHIBUYA SKY
about: SHIBUYA SKY is an observation facility on the top floors and rooftop of Shibuya Scramble Square, directly connected to Shibuya Station. It includes indoor galleries on the 45th and 46th floors and an open-air rooftop with a 360-degree view. The facility opened in November 2019. Entry is by time-slot ticket, and visitors can stay as long as they like after entering. The rooftop may close in bad weather.
closed: January 1; may close temporarily on some other days
price: Adults from 2,700 yen online (depends on the time slot); 3,000-3,700 yen at the counter; children under 5 free
station: Shibuya Station (directly connected)
parking: No parking in the building; paid parking nearby
car: Not recommended; public transport is easier

name: Akihabara Electric Town
about: Akihabara is centered on Akihabara Station and is known as Electric Town. Its electronics trade grew from a black market after World War II, and from the 1980s shops shifted toward computers, anime, manga and games. Today the area has large electronics stores, game centers, hobby and anime shops, and maid cafes. Chuo-dori is closed to cars on some afternoons for pedestrians.
hours: Open all day as a district; most shops about 10:00-20:00 (each shop sets its own hours)
price: Free to walk
station: Akihabara Station (JR Yamanote Line, JR Keihin-Tohoku Line, JR Chuo-Sobu Line, Hibiya Line, Tsukuba Express)
car: Possible, but public transport is easier

name: Ueno Park
about: Ueno Onshi Park is a large public park that is home to several museums, Ueno Zoo and Shinobazu Pond with its Bentendo hall. Museums in the park include the Tokyo National Museum, the National Museum of Western Art and the National Museum of Nature and Science. The park is known for cherry blossoms in spring. The park is free to enter, while the museums and zoo have their own fees and hours.
hours: 5:00-23:00 (museums and the zoo have their own hours)
closed: Open daily (museums are mostly closed on Mondays)
price: Free (museums and zoo charge separately)
station: Ueno Station (JR lines, Ginza Line, Hibiya Line), Park Exit
car: Possible, but public transport is easier

name: Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden
about: Shinjuku Gyoen is a national garden of 58.3 hectares combining Japanese, English landscape and French formal garden styles. The land was granted to the Naito family in 1590, became an imperial botanical garden in 1879, and was reopened in 1906. Most of the garden was damaged by air raids in 1945, and it reopened as a national garden in 1949. It is known for cherry blossoms in spring and chrysanthemums in autumn.
hours: Oct 1-Mar 14: 9:00-16:30; Mar 15-Jun 10 and Aug 1-Sep 30: 9:00-18:00; Jun 11-Jul 31: 9:00-19:00 (last entry 30 minutes before closing)
closed: Mondays (next day if Monday is a holiday; open during cherry blossom and chrysanthemum seasons); Dec 29-Jan 3
price: Adults 500 yen; 65 and over and students 250 yen; junior high school age and under free
station: Shinjuku-gyoemmae Station (Marunouchi Line)
car: Not recommended; no parking at the garden

name: Mt. Takao
about: Mt. Takao is a 599-meter mountain in Hachioji, about an hour from central Tokyo by train. Several marked trails lead to the summit, and a cable car and chair lift run partway up. Yakuo-in, a Buddhist temple on the mountain, is a popular stop. The summit has views toward Mt. Fuji on clear days. Hiking is free, and the cable car and lift cost 490 yen one way.
hours: Trails open daily; cable car about 8:00-17:45 (varies by season)
closed: Open daily (cable car has maintenance days)
price: Free to hike; cable car or chair lift 490 yen one way, 980 yen round trip
station: Takaosanguchi Station (Keio Takao Line)
car: Possible, but weekends are crowded; trains are easier

name: Yoyogi Park
about: Yoyogi Park is a large public park next to Harajuku, on land once used as the Olympic Village for the 1964 Tokyo Games. It has wide lawns, tree-lined paths, a pond and a cherry blossom area. On weekends people picnic, play sports and play music. Some facilities in the park have their own hours.
hours: Open 24 hours (facilities have their own hours)
price: Free
station: Harajuku Station (JR Yamanote Line); Yoyogi-koen Station (Chiyoda Line)
car: Possible, but public transport is easier

name: Showa Kinen Park
about: Showa Kinen Park is a national park of about 180 hectares in Tachikawa and Akishima, opened to mark the 50th year of Emperor Showa's reign. It has wide lawns, a Japanese garden, a flower field and bicycle rental. It is known for flowers through the seasons and for autumn leaves. Hours are longer on weekends in summer and during some autumn events.
hours: 9:30-17:00 (Apr-Sep weekends and holidays to 18:00; Nov-Feb 9:30-16:30); longer during events
closed: Dec 31 and Jan 1; some days in late January and February (check the calendar)
price: Adults 450 yen, ages 65 and over 210 yen, junior high school students and under free
station: Nishi-Tachikawa Station (JR Ome Line); Tachikawa Station (JR Chuo Line)
car: Possible, with paid parking

name: Inokashira Park
about: Inokashira Park is a park around a pond that is the source of the Kanda River, a short walk from Kichijoji Station. Visitors rent rowboats and swan pedal boats on the pond, and cherry trees along its edge bloom in spring. The park also has a small zoo and a shrine to Benzaiten. Boats and the zoo charge separately.
hours: Open all day (facilities have their own hours)
price: Free (boats and zoo charge separately)
station: Kichijoji Station (JR Chuo Line, Keio Inokashira Line)
car: Possible, but public transport is easier

name: Hamarikyu Gardens
about: Hamarikyu Gardens is a Japanese landscape garden beside Tokyo Bay, built on the site of a feudal lord's residence and later used by the shogunal family. It has a tidal pond fed by seawater, with a teahouse on an island where visitors can have matcha and a sweet. The garden is surrounded by skyscrapers from the Shiodome area. It was opened to the public in 1946.
price: Adults 300 yen, ages 65 and over 150 yen; free on May 4 and Oct 1
station: Shiodome Station (Oedo Line, Yurikamome Line); Tsukijishijo Station (Oedo Line)
car: Not recommended; no parking at the garden

name: Rikugien Gardens
about: Rikugien was created by Yoshiyasu Yanagisawa, an adviser to the shogun Tsunayoshi Tokugawa. The name means Garden of Six Poems, and it was designed to depict 88 scenes from classical poems. Stone markers show the scenes, though only 32 remain. A hill gives a view over the whole garden. It is known for cherry blossoms in spring and maples in autumn, with evening illuminations in both seasons.
hours: 9:00-17:00 (last entry 16:30); evening illumination hours vary
price: Adults 300 yen; free on May 4 and Oct 1
station: Komagome Station (JR Yamanote Line, Namboku Line)
car: Not recommended; no parking at the garden

name: Kiyosumi Gardens
about: Kiyosumi Gardens is a stroll garden built around a central pond, with stepping stones across the water and rocks collected from all over Japan. It was developed in the Meiji era by Iwasaki Yataro, the founder of Mitsubishi, and later donated to the city. It opened to the public in 1932. The pond is home to turtles and many waterbirds.
price: Adults 150 yen, ages 65 and over 70 yen; free on May 4 and Oct 1
station: Kiyosumi-shirakawa Station (Oedo Line, Hanzomon Line)
car: Not recommended; no parking at the garden

name: Koishikawa Korakuen Gardens
about: Koishikawa Korakuen is a landscape garden built in the early Edo period at the Tokyo residence of the Mito branch of the Tokugawa family. It recreates famous Japanese and Chinese scenery in miniature with ponds, stones, trees and artificial hills. The name comes from a poem about a ruler finding pleasure only after the people's happiness. The garden sits beside Tokyo Dome.
price: Adults 300 yen; free on May 4 and Oct 1
station: Iidabashi Station (JR Chuo-Sobu Line, Tozai, Yurakucho, Namboku, Oedo lines); Suidobashi Station (JR Chuo-Sobu Line)
car: Not recommended; no parking at the garden
